questions.stem:
1. Rachel is an excellent high school student who earns high grades in challenging classes. She has recently been hired as a part-time lab assistant at a medical clinic. She is concerned that the job will affect her school performance.

Part A
Provide a specific example that clearly illustrates how each of the following would inhibit Rachel's success at her new job.
• Stereotype threat
• Adrenal glands
• Lack of REM sleep

Part B
Provide a specific example that clearly illustrates how each of the following would enhance her performance as a student with a challenging academic schedule.
• Distributed practice
• Reciprocal determinism
• Self-efficacy
notes: Prompt transcribed from assets/psychology/papers/2017/2017.pdf.
Rubric parts were structured from the official scoring guidelines; no rubric points were invented.

questions.stem:
2. Thirty-year-old Kent found a bag containing several thousand dollars in a park. He is discussing with his family whether to give the money to the appropriate authorities or to keep the money.
Explain how each of the following psychological concepts could influence Kent's decision-making process.
• Prefrontal cortex
• Postconventional moral reasoning
• Antisocial personality disorder
• Evolutionary psychology
• Cognitive dissonance
• Incentive theory
• Groupthink
notes: Prompt transcribed from assets/psychology/papers/2017/2017.pdf.
Rubric parts were structured from the official scoring guidelines; no rubric points were invented.

frq_rubrics.general_considerations:
1. Answers must be presented in sentences, and sentences must be cogent enough for the meaning of the response to come through. Spelling and grammatical mistakes do not reduce the score of a response, but spelling must be close enough that the reader is convinced of the word.
2. Do not score any notes made on the question section of the booklet. Score only what has been written in the blanks provided in the booklet.
3. Definitions alone will not score, but they may be used to enhance the application.
4. Within a point, a student will not be penalized for misinformation unless it directly contradicts correct information that would otherwise have scored a point. A correct application with incorrect definition is not considered a direct contradiction and should score the point.
5. Rubric examples provided for each point are not to be considered exhaustive.
6. Responses that simply parrot or repeat the terms from the question will not score.
7. A response can score point only if it clearly conveys what part of the question is being answered. It is possible to infer what part of the question is being answered if it is consistent with the order of the question.

parts.label: Point 1
parts.title: Stereotype threat
parts.criteria: Rachel’s job performance may be inhibited if she is confronted with or aware of stereotypical beliefs that the job is difficult for a specified population or category to which she belongs (gender, age, or ethnicity).
examples_positive: If Rachel is told high school students are not mature enough for a medical setting, she may question her ability and make mistakes.
Because Rachel knows more men work in medicine, she may think she is not as good as male lab assistants and decide to quit.
examples_negative: Examples of discrimination or stereotypes alone do not score.
parts.notes: Part A responses must refer to inhibiting job performance, not school performance, for points 1-3.

parts.label: Point 2
parts.title: Adrenal glands
parts.criteria: Adrenal gland activity could inhibit Rachel’s performance: if she becomes too aroused or not aroused enough, her performance is impaired by nervousness, anxiety, or stress.
examples_positive: Rachel’s anxiety causes her adrenal glands to release hormones, heightening arousal and making concentration harder.
If her adrenal glands do not secrete enough noradrenaline, she may lack the alertness needed for the job.
parts.notes: Students do not have to specify a hormone.

parts.label: Point 3
parts.title: Lack of REM sleep
parts.criteria: REM sleep is key for forming and consolidating new memories. Without REM sleep, Rachel has trouble processing and recalling information important for job performance.
examples_positive: Without REM sleep, Rachel has difficulty processing what she learned and makes mistakes at work.
parts.notes: The impairment should not be attributed to sleep deprivation alone.

parts.label: Point 4
parts.title: Distributed practice
parts.criteria: The response indicates studying that is spaced or spread over multiple time periods and enhances school or job performance.
examples_positive: Rachel studied the material a little bit each day during the semester.
Rachel studies in intervals, which helps her remember the material better.
examples_negative: Studying over a long period of time without spacing does not score.
Grouping or chunking without spaced practice does not score.
“Spaced out” or “spread out” without multiple time periods does not score.

parts.label: Point 5
parts.title: Reciprocal determinism
parts.criteria: The response must include all three elements—personal factors, behaviors, and environmental setting—and indicate enhanced school or job performance.
examples_positive: Because Rachel is conscientious, she organizes her study time efficiently, works longer at the clinic, and learns procedures more quickly.
Rachel is an extravert, seeks out teachers for help, and improves her understanding.

parts.label: Point 6
parts.title: Self-efficacy
parts.criteria: The response must reflect a belief, knowledge, or expectancy in one’s ability to perform a behavior or task, and connect that belief to success at school or work.
examples_positive: Rachel knows she can balance school and work, which leads to greater success.
Rachel believes she can learn anything, so she masters tasks quickly in the lab.
examples_negative: Self-confidence, efficiency, self-esteem, or internal locus of control without reference to a belief does not score.

notes: Official scoring guidelines; points are 0/1.

frq_rubrics.general_considerations:
1. Answers must be presented in sentences, and sentences must be cogent enough for the meaning of the response to come through. Spelling and grammatical mistakes do not reduce the score of a response, but spelling must be close enough that the reader is convinced of the word.
2. Do not score any notes made on the question section of the booklet. Score only what has been written in the blanks provided in the booklet.
3. Definitions alone will not score, but they may be used to enhance the application.
4. Within a point, a student will not be penalized for misinformation unless it directly contradicts correct information that would otherwise have scored a point. A correct application with incorrect definition is not considered a direct contradiction and should score the point.
5. Rubric examples provided for each point are not to be considered exhaustive.
6. Responses that simply parrot or repeat the terms from the question will not score.
7. A response can score point only if it clearly conveys what part of the question is being answered. It is possible to infer what part of the question is being answered if it is consistent with the order of the question.
8. To score, each concept must be discussed in the context of Kent's deciding to either keep or return the money.

parts.label: Point 1
parts.title: Prefrontal cortex
parts.criteria: The response describes at least one prefrontal cortex function (planning, reasoning, decision making, judgment, attention, empathy) and ties it to Kent’s situation.
examples_positive: By deciding to keep the money, Kent is using his prefrontal cortex, which is used for decision making.
examples_negative: A definition alone, such as “the prefrontal cortex is the ability to make good decisions,” does not score.
If decision making is used, the function and application must be distinct; a non-brain area responsible for decision making does not score.

parts.label: Point 2
parts.title: Postconventional moral reasoning
parts.criteria: The response explains that this stage reflects universal or abstract ethical principles, such as the greater good or justice, rather than simply following rules or avoiding punishment and rewards.
examples_positive: He is able to think about this ethical dilemma abstractly and keeps the money.

parts.label: Point 3
parts.title: Antisocial personality disorder
parts.criteria: The response explains that someone with this disorder has increased impulsivity and hedonism, or lacks guilt, empathy, or regard for the rights of others, and describes how the presence or absence of ASPD affects Kent’s decision.
examples_positive: Keith, Kent’s brother, has ASPD and lacks empathy, and convinces Kent not to return the money.
examples_negative: “Because Kent is shy, he will not tell the police” does not score.

parts.label: Point 4
parts.title: Evolutionary psychology
parts.criteria: The response explains that the behavior was evolutionarily selected in previous generations, or contributes to survival of the species, including passing on genes or increasing offspring survival.
examples_positive: If Kent’s family is poor, he keeps the money to help ensure the family survives.
Kent gives back the money because his ancestors were moral and he has that gene.
examples_negative: “Survival of the fittest” leading Kent to keep money to buy food does not score.
“Humans change over time” or selfishness alone does not score.
parts.notes: Responses that include reciprocal helping do score.

parts.label: Point 5
parts.title: Cognitive dissonance
parts.criteria: The response explains both the discrepancy between thoughts and/or behaviors and the anxiety, discomfort, or uneasiness that comes from that discrepancy.
examples_positive: Kent felt stress because he knew he should give back the money but also knew he could really use it for college.
examples_negative: Describing the discrepancy alone does not score.
Family disappointment without the dissonance experience does not score.

parts.label: Point 6
parts.title: Incentive theory
parts.criteria: Extrinsic or external rewards have a direct impact on behavior. The incentive may favor keeping or returning the money, but it must be something other than the found money itself.
examples_positive: Suzy tells Kent she will go on a date with him if he keeps the money, so he keeps it.
Because the authorities have not offered a finder’s fee, Kent does not return the money.
examples_negative: “Due to incentive theory, Kent keeps the money as a reward” does not score.

parts.label: Point 7
parts.title: Groupthink
parts.criteria: Kent’s decision making is impaired or affected because the family discussion is driven by maintaining consensus or group harmony rather than critical or rational thinking. Attempts to avoid groupthink also score.
examples_positive: Kent wants to make a good decision, but everyone seems to agree rather than think logically.
Kent asks family members to give honest opinions even if they get mad, because he wants the best decision.
examples_negative: The family simply agreeing that Kent should keep the money does not score.

notes: Official scoring guidelines; points are 0/1.
